<reason>Genuinely close, high-skill debate. A's deterrence core was the heaviest impact and was never fully closed — B's screening and request apparatus sits downstream of a door the deterred young adult never walks through, and B's alternative channels carry knowledge and means burdens A pressed well. But B won more of the contested ground: the default-vs-trigger distinction cleanly neutralized A's flashiest move ("the fixes are the motion"), B converted A's candid "protects her from nothing" concession into a structural narrowing of A's case, landed an unanswered tu quoque (A trusts clinician judgment for imminent-risk exceptions, so it can't dismiss clinician screening), and counter-framed A's closing with "it counts only half the silence." B also executed flawlessly while A was clipped twice and A's closing kept attacking the outdated patient-initiated version of B's safeguard rather than the refined proactive-screening version. Competitive throughout, but B adapted better and left fewer loose ends.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1: the default-vs-trigger distinction ("a confidential-communication request is triggered when there is a reason; the motion makes concealment the automatic default... keyed to nothing but age") defused A's strongest attack, and the follow-up pressure question set the concession trap that let B argue the motion rested entirely on an already-protected population — the sequence that most shaped the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
